propositions.text: This is an application for judicial review of an immigration officer's decision refusing the Applicant's permanent residence application.
propositions.quote: This is an application for judicial review of the decision of an immigration officer of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (“Officer”), dated August 10, 2016, refusing the Applicant’s application for permanent residence

propositions.text: The refusal was based on failure to meet IRP Regulations requirements due to no qualifying offer of permanent employment.
propositions.quote: on the basis that the Applicant failed to meet the requirements of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227 (“IRP Regulations”) as he did not provide a qualifying offer of permanent employment.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review application of an immigration officer's refusal of the Applicant's permanent residence for lack of qualifying employment.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is dismissed.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, this application for judicial review is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the judicial review application.

propositions.text: The Applicant is an Indian citizen who studied in Canada and worked at Horizon Travel Magazine as a web designer starting October 2014.
propositions.quote: The Applicant is a citizen of India. Upon completing certificates of study in Canada, he obtained a post-graduate work permit (“PGWP”) and began working at Horizon Travel Magazine (“Horizon”) as a web designer in October 2014.

propositions.text: The Applicant's PGWP was renewed to July 2016 and Horizon applied for an LMIA on his behalf, approved October 27, 2015.
propositions.quote: His PGWP was subsequently renewed to July 2016. In June 2015, Horizon applied for a Labour Market Impact Assessment (“LMIA”) on the Applicant’s behalf, which was approved on October 27, 2015.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant is an Indian citizen who worked in Canada with a renewed PGWP and had an LMIA approved for him.

propositions.text: The Applicant submitted an Express Entry profile in September 2015 indicating a qualifying offer of arranged employment.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submitted his profile to the Citizenship and Immigration Canada Express Entry intake system in September 2015, indicating that he had a qualifying offer of arranged employment.

propositions.text: He received an invitation to apply for permanent residency with 971 points including 600 for arranged employment.
propositions.quote: On November 27, 2015, the Applicant received an invitation to apply for permanent residency as a Federal Skilled Worker. The invitation indicated that the Applicant qualified for 971 points, including 600 for having arranged employment.

propositions.text: The Applicant applied for permanent residency on January 22, 2016, but the application was returned incomplete for missing medical and education documents.
propositions.quote: The Applicant made an application for permanent residency on January 22, 2016, and included his LMIA confirmation number in the application. This application was returned as incomplete on January 28, 2016 as the Applicant had not provided the required medical report and proof of education documents.

propositions.text: He resubmitted and received a second invitation on February 10, 2016, submitting LMIA approval and a January 18, 2015 letter from Horizon confirming employment.
propositions.quote: He resubmitted his profile and received a second invitation to apply for permanent residency on February 10, 2016. When submitting the required supporting documentation, the Applicant included the LMIA approval letter and a January 18, 2015 letter from Horizon confirming his employment as of October 2014.

propositions.text: The Applicant finalized submission in February 2016; application was refused on August 10, 2016.
propositions.quote: He uploaded his documents and finalised his submission in February 2016. On August 10, 2016, his application was refused.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the Applicant's Express Entry profile, invitations, submissions, and refusal of permanent residency application.

propositions.text: The Officer refused the application under s 11.2 IRPA for lack of qualifying offer of arranged employment.
propositions.quote: In the refusal letter of August 10, 2016 the Officer stated that, pursuant to s 11.2 of the Immigration Refugee and Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 (“IRPA”), an officer may not issue a visa in respect of an application for permanent residence if the applicant who had been issued an invitation to make such an application does not have the qualifications on the basis of which they were ranked

propositions.text: The Officer was not satisfied the Applicant had a permanent employment offer meeting IRP Regulations requirements.
propositions.quote: The Officer stated that he or she was not satisfied that the Applicant met the requirements of the IRP Regulations because he did not provide an offer of employment offering him a permanent position in Canada.

propositions.text: The Officer found the Applicant lost points and rank below the lowest invited person due to lack of qualifying offer.
propositions.quote: The change in his qualification resulted in a loss of points that brought his rank below the lowest ranking person invited to apply under the Express Entry Comprehensive Ranking System.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the Officer refused the application for lack of a qualifying permanent employment offer, causing loss of points and rank.

propositions.text: GCMS Notes form part of the decision reasons and indicate the Applicant did not submit an offer of employment despite LMIA approval.
propositions.quote: The Global Case Management System notes (“GCMS Notes”) form a part of the reasons for the decision ... PA did not submit an offer of employment.

propositions.text: The January 18, 2015 letter confirmed employment start date, position, and salary but lacked duties; Officer was not satisfied of qualifying offer.
propositions.quote: The letter dated 2015/01/18 provides information about PA’s employment starting date, position and annual salary; duties are not listed. I am not satisfied that PA has a qualifying offer of employment.

propositions.text: The Applicant's CRS score dropped from 971 to 371, below the minimum 459, leading to refusal under R82(1) and A11.2.
propositions.quote: CRS SCORE AT ITA: 971 REVISED CRS SCORE: 371 MINIMUM CRS SCORE FOR THIS ROUND: 459... I am therefore not satisfied that PA has a qualifying job offer according to R82(1) or that PA meets A11.2 - refused.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes GCMS evidence shows no qualifying offer submitted, leading to score drop and refusal under regulations.

propositions.text: The Applicant raises two issues: breach of procedural fairness and reasonableness of the Officer's decision.
propositions.quote: The Applicant raises two issues. The first is whether the Officer breached the duty of procedural fairness. The second is whether the Officer’s decision is reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant's two issues: procedural fairness breach and reasonableness of decision.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness regarding failure to notify applicant of concerns is reviewable on correctness standard.
propositions.quote: Whether a visa officer erred by failing to bring his or her concerns to the attention of an applicant and offering the applicant an opportunity to address them is a question of procedural fairness which is reviewable on the correctness standard

paragraphs.summary: The court states procedural fairness questions are reviewed on correctness standard.

propositions.text: Reasonableness is the standard for reviewing officer's assessment of permanent residence applications under Federal Skilled Worker Program.
propositions.quote: The standard of review that applies to an officer’s assessment of an application for permanent residence under the Federal Skilled Worker Program ... is reasonableness

propositions.text: Officer's assessment is entitled to high deference.
propositions.quote: An officer’s assessment in that regard is entitled to a high degree of deference

paragraphs.summary: The court states reasonableness is the standard for reviewing officer's assessment, with high deference.

propositions.text: Reasonableness requires justification, transparency, intelligibility, and defensible outcomes in facts and law.
propositions.quote: Reasonableness is concerned with the existence of justification, transparency and intelligibility within the decision-making process but also with whether the decision falls within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes which are defensible in respect of the facts and law

propositions.text: Dunsmuir defines reasonableness as justification, transparency, intelligibility, and defensible outcomes.
propositions.quote: Dunsmuir at para 47

paragraphs.summary: The court explains reasonableness requires justification, transparency, intelligibility, and defensible outcomes, citing Dunsmuir.

propositions.text: LMIA approval letter was sufficient evidence of qualifying permanent offer of arranged employment.
propositions.quote: The Applicant makes two submissions in this regard. The first is that the LMIA approval letter was sufficient evidence that he had a qualifying and permanent offer of arranged employment.

propositions.text: Duty of fairness requires officers to ask questions when concerns about credibility or genuineness arise.
propositions.quote: The duty of fairness requires officers to ask appropriate questions of applicants when they have concerns about the credibility, accuracy, or genuine nature of information that otherwise would be sufficient, if believed.

propositions.text: Concerns about existence or genuineness of offer or ability to carry out employment should have been put to Applicant.
propositions.quote: Thus, any concerns about the existence or genuineness of the offer, or the ability of the Applicant to carry out the employment, should have been put to the Applicant.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues LMIA letter suffices as evidence and fairness requires officers to question concerns about genuineness.

propositions.text: Officer has no duty to assist applicant or advise of concerns from insufficient evidence if no credibility issues.
propositions.quote: The Respondent says that, barring credibility or authenticity concerns, the Officer was under no duty to assist the Applicant in his application for permanent residence. There is no duty to advise an applicant of concerns which arise from the applicant having failed to submit sufficient evidence meeting regulatory requirements.

propositions.text: Officer was not satisfied Applicant had qualifying offer but did not question credibility of evidence.
propositions.quote: Here, the Officer did not question the credibility of the Applicant’s evidence, but was not satisfied that the Applicant had a qualifying offer of employment.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues no duty to assist or advise absent credibility concerns; Officer was not satisfied but did not question credibility.

propositions.text: The matter is sufficiency of evidence and reasonableness of Officer's conclusion on qualifying offer.
propositions.quote: In my view, this matter is really a question of the sufficiency of the evidence and, in that regard, the reasonableness of the Officer’s conclusion that the Applicant had not demonstrated that he had a qualifying offer of employment.

propositions.text: The Officer's finding was not unreasonable.
propositions.quote: As set out below, I do not believe that finding was unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the issue is evidence sufficiency and the Officer's conclusion was reasonable.

propositions.text: No obligation on visa officer to provide opportunity to address concerns when documents are incomplete or insufficient.
propositions.quote: there is no obligation on a visa officer to provide an applicant with an opportunity to address concerns of the officer when the supporting documents are incomplete, unclear or insufficient to satisfy the officer that the applicant meets all the requirements

propositions.text: Cites Pathirannahelage, Hamza, Gharialia, Veryamani, Rezvani for no duty to assist on insufficient evidence.
propositions.quote: see also Hamza at paras 24-25; Gharialia v Canada ... Veryamani v Canada ... Rezvani v Canada ...

paragraphs.summary: The court states visa officers have no duty to assist applicants when documents are incomplete or insufficient, citing precedents.

propositions.text: Visa officers not obligated to convey concerns arising from IRP Regulations or sufficiency of evidence.
propositions.quote: visa officers are not obligated to convey concerns that arise from the requirements of the IRP Regulations or deal with sufficiency of evidence.

propositions.text: Cites Gedara and Virk cases supporting no duty to seek missing evidence or advise on sufficiency.
propositions.quote: as noted by Justice Manson in Gedara ... In Virk ... Justice Barnes noted ...

propositions.text: Justice Barnes found no breach of procedural fairness where applicant failed to provide required evidence and officer required more.
propositions.quote: There is no breach of procedural fairness in these circumstances and the Officer’s finding that an essential aspect of the proposed employment was missing was reasonable…

paragraphs.summary: The court explains visa officers have no duty to advise on sufficiency or seek missing evidence, citing Gedara and Virk.

propositions.text: No record suggests Officer had concerns about genuineness of application or documents.
propositions.quote: there is nothing in the record suggesting that the Officer had any concerns about the genuineness of the application.

propositions.text: Distinction between disregarding evidence for genuineness doubts and finding evidence insufficient on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: There is a distinction between disregarding evidence due to doubts as to its genuineness or reliability and finding that evidence is insufficient to prove a fact on a balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: Officer found documents insufficient to prove qualifying offer for indeterminate period and no duty to advise Applicant of insufficiency.
propositions.quote: In this matter the Officer found that the documents submitted were insufficient to prove that the Applicant had a qualifying offer of employment for an indeterminate period. ... There was no duty on the Officer to advise the Applicant of his or her concerns regarding the insufficiency of the evidence submitted.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no genuineness concerns, distinguishes insufficiency from credibility, and finds no duty to advise on insufficiency.

propositions.text: Applicant claims procedural unfairness because application was refused, not returned incomplete, contrary to legitimate expectations.
propositions.quote: the Applicant submits that the decision was procedurally unfair because his application was refused rather than returned to him as incomplete, contrary to his legitimate expectations.

propositions.text: Applicant argues legitimate expectation based on FSW Processing Manual, IRP Regulations ss 10(1)(c) and 12, and prior incomplete return.
propositions.quote: This expectation is allegedly based on the FSW Processing Manual and ss 10(1)(c) and 12 of the IRP Regulations and because his initial application was returned as incomplete when he did not provide a medical report or proof of education documents with the application.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues refusal rather than return was procedurally unfair, based on legitimate expectations from manuals and regulations.

propositions.text: Respondent says legitimate expectations doctrine confers only procedural rights, not substantive rights like avoiding refusal.
propositions.quote: the doctrine confers only procedural rights. The Respondent submits that passing the initial check for document completeness cannot shield an applicant from being found, at the second stage, to have insufficient or no evidence to meet a regulatory requirement.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues legitimate expectations only confer procedural rights, not substantive rights to avoid refusal.

propositions.text: Applicant submitted documents for all required categories, so application was complete but documents insufficient to meet regulatory requirements.
propositions.quote: Here it appears that the Applicant did submit documents for all required categories, including the offer of employment category, and, in this sense, the application was “complete.” The Officer found, however, that the documents provided were insufficient to establish that the Applicant met the regulatory requirements

propositions.text: This differs from prior incomplete return for missing medical and education documents.
propositions.quote: This is distinguishable from the Applicant’s prior submission when his application was returned as incomplete because he did not provide documents under the required categories of medical report or proof of education with the application submission.

propositions.text: Doctrine of legitimate expectations does not apply in these circumstances.
propositions.quote: The doctrine of legitimate expectations has no application in these circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the application was complete but documents insufficient, distinguishing prior incomplete return, and rejects legitimate expectations claim.

propositions.text: Applicant submits LMIA approval letter is sufficient evidence of qualifying permanent offer of arranged employment.
propositions.quote: While the Applicant does not address this matter through a reasonableness lens ... he submitted that the LMIA approval letter was sufficient evidence that he had a qualifying and permanent offer of arranged employment.

propositions.text: LMIA validates offer of employment under IRP Regulations ss 82(2), 203 and 315.2.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits the presence of an LMIA clearly supports that an offer of employment existed, as the purpose of an LMIA application is to validate an offer of employment made to a skilled worker as reflected in ss 82(2), 203 and 315.2 of the IRP Regulations.

propositions.text: LMIA approval letter lists employer, Applicant's name, position, and continuous full-time permanent employment.
propositions.quote: Further, the approval letter itself clearly listed Horizon as the employer, the Applicant’s name, the nature of the position, and that the Applicant was being offered continuous, full-time employment of permanent/indeterminate length.

propositions.text: Applicant agrees LMIA not determinative; visa officers can deny if concerns about ability or likelihood to perform employment exist, but no such concerns here.
propositions.quote: Although the Applicant agrees that an LMIA is not determinative of whether a visa should be issued ... he submits that no such concerns were raised in this matter.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues LMIA letter suffices as evidence of qualifying permanent employment and no concerns about ability or likelihood were raised.

propositions.text: No legislative basis requires an offer of employment; it's only a policy requirement, so failure to provide it can't disqualify him
propositions.quote: there is no legislative basis upon which an offer of employment is required. This is simply a policy requirement and therefore, failure to provide an offer of employment cannot disqualify him.

propositions.text: Officer accepted he had an offer of permanent employment by awarding 600 points for arranged employment
propositions.quote: because he had already been awarded 971 points, 600 of which were awarded for having arranged employment, the Officer had accepted that the Applicant had an offer of permanent employment in Canada

propositions.text: LMIA post-dated invitation but was valid when points awarded; offer of employment requirement is backwards looking
propositions.quote: His LMIA post-dated his invitation and was valid when the points were awarded; providing an offer of employment was therefore backwards looking.

propositions.text: January 18, 2015 letter proves he had employment; LMIA proves he had an offer of permanent employment which Officer failed to appreciate
propositions.quote: The January 18, 2015 letter of employment only served to prove that he had employment, while the LMIA proved he had an offer of permanent employment which the Officer failed to appreciate.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues no legislative basis requires offer of employment; Officer accepted offer by awarding points; LMIA valid when points awarded; January 18 letter proves employment, LMIA proves offer.

propositions.text: Visa officers are not bound by LMIA checks from Employment and Social Development Canada
propositions.quote: The Respondent agrees that visa officers are not bound by LMIA checks produced by Employment and Social Development Canada.

propositions.text: Applicant was advised to include a job offer signed by him and employer; such offer is not superfluous or unreasonable to require
propositions.quote: the Applicant was advised in his Express Entry document checklist to include a job offer signed by him and his employer. Such a job offer cannot be considered superfluous, nor can it be considered unreasonable for an immigration officer to look for an offer

propositions.text: January 18, 2015 letter did not state position was permanent, so officer could note this deficiency
propositions.quote: the letter that was uploaded, dated January 18, 2015, did not contain this information.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent says visa officers not bound by LMIA; job offer signed by applicant and employer required; January 18 letter lacked permanent position info.

propositions.text: LMIA is not a rubber stamp for permanent residency; it allows points to be assessed and invitation issued if points sufficient
propositions.quote: The LMIA is not a rubber stamp for permanent residency. It allows qualifying points to be assessed and, if the points are sufficient, an invitation to apply for permanent residency may be issued.

propositions.text: Express Entry checklist is policy-prescribed; letter of offer content clearly described; Applicant failed to submit required document
propositions.quote: the Express Entry document checklist is prescribed by policy, the content of the letter of offer from an employer is clearly described. The Applicant simply failed to submit a document that met the requirements.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues LMIA not automatic for residency; checklist prescribes letter content; Applicant failed to submit required letter.

propositions.text: Applicant required to satisfy Officer that s 82 IRP Regulations criteria met, meaning employer offered arranged employment
propositions.quote: Applicant was required to satisfy the Officer that the criteria in s 82 of the IRP Regulations were met

propositions.text: s 82 IRP Regulations defines arranged employment as offer for continuous full-time work at least one year after visa issuance
propositions.quote: In s 82(1) “arranged employment” is defined as an offer of employment “for continuous full-time work in Canada having a duration of at least one year after the date on which a permanent resident visa is issued”

propositions.text: Plain reading of s 82 requires submission of an offer of employment
propositions.quote: On plain reading, this required the submission of an offer of employment.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Applicant must satisfy s 82 IRP Regulations requiring offer of employment for continuous full-time work at least one year after visa issuance.

propositions.text: LMIA approval letter states foreign worker needs LMIA letter and Annex A to apply for work permit or permanent resident visa before LMIA expiry
propositions.quote: The foreign worker requires a copy of this LMIA letter and Annex A to apply to Citizenship and Immigration Canada (CIC) for their work permit or permanent resident visa, and must apply prior to the LMIA expiry date stated in the annex.

propositions.text: CIC requires employment contract or job offer letter signed by employer and foreign worker before issuing work permit or permanent resident visa
propositions.quote: CIC will also need the foreign worker to submit a copy of the employment contract or job offer letter (if applicable to the program stream), signed by the employer and the foreign worker, prior to issuing a work permit or permanent resident visa.

propositions.text: LMIA does not authorize entry, stay or work; it is only one CIC requirement to issue permit or visa
propositions.quote: The LMIA does not authorize the foreign worker(s) to enter, remain or work in Canada; it is only one of CIC’s requirements to determine whether or not to issue a work permit or permanent resident visa.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes LMIA letter requires employment contract signed by employer and worker before permit or visa issued; LMIA alone doesn't authorize entry or work.

propositions.text: Express Entry document checklist is personalized and identifies specific supporting documents required
propositions.quote: a personalized document checklist is produced for each applicant when they submit the application through their online account, which identifies the specific supporting documents required.

propositions.text: Letter of offer confirms qualifying arranged employment and screens for fraud; required if applicant claims arranged employment
propositions.quote: the purpose of the letter is to confirm an applicant’s qualifying offer of arranged employment to validate that the applicant meets the program requirements and to screen for concerns of fraud. It states that the document is required only if, as in this case, the applicant claims to have a qualifying offer of arranged employment.

propositions.text: Letter must be on company letterhead, include specified details like start date, full-time work for at least one year, job title, duties, salary, benefits
propositions.quote: a letter from the employer offering the job in Canada is required, it must be printed on company letterhead and, include the specified information. It must also include the following specified details: the expected start date; commitment that the applicant will be employed on a continuous, paid, full-time work basis, for work that is for at least one year after issuance of a permanent resident visa; job title; duties and responsibilities; current job status (if current job); number of work hours per week and annual salary plus benefits.

propositions.text: If LMIA associated, LMIA number requested; scanned LMIA copy not required initially but may be requested later
propositions.quote: If there is an associated LMIA to the offer of employment, the LMIA number is requested as a part of the application. A scanned copy of the LMIA is not required when submitting the application but may be requested at a later date.

paragraphs.summary: Court describes Express Entry checklist requires letter of offer with detailed info; LMIA number requested but scanned copy not initially required.

propositions.text: Applicant provided LMIA approval letter as offer and January 18, 2015 letter as letter of employment
propositions.quote: Applicant provided the LMIA approval letter as his offer of employment and the January 18, 2015 letter from Horizon as his letter of employment.

propositions.text: Officer noted valid LMIA and January 18 letter but not satisfied Applicant had qualifying offer confirming permanent position
propositions.quote: Officer noted that the Applicant had a valid LMIA and considered the January 18, 2015 letter, but was not satisfied the Applicant had a qualifying offer of employment because the Applicant did not provide an offer of employment confirming a permanent position in Canada.

propositions.text: January 18 letter states Applicant employed since October 2014 as web developer with salary but does not show forward-looking offer signed by both parties
propositions.quote: The January 18, 2015 letter states that Horizon confirms that the Applicant has been employed with Horizon since October 2014 and currently holds the position of web developer and sets out his salary for that position. Thus, the January 18, 2015 does not demonstrate that Applicant had a forward-looking offer of employment for continuous, full-time work signed by both the Applicant and the employer.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant gave LMIA and January 18 letter; Officer noted LMIA but not satisfied offer confirmed permanent position; January 18 letter shows past employment only.

propositions.text: Applicant's affidavit includes June 19, 2015 letter offering permanent full-time position signed by both parties
propositions.quote: Applicant included as an exhibit his LMIA application, including a June 19, 2015 offer of employment letter from Horizon offering him a permanent full-time position as a web developer and setting out his duties. The letter was signed by Horizon and the Applicant.

propositions.text: June 19, 2015 letter was not provided with permanent residence application and not before Officer when decision made
propositions.quote: that letter was not provided with his application for permanent residence and was not before the Officer when he or she made their decision to reject his application.

propositions.text: Evidentiary record on judicial review is restricted to record before decision-maker; new evidence generally inadmissible
propositions.quote: As a general rule, the evidentiary record before this Court on judicial review is restricted to the evidentiary record that was before the decision-maker.

propositions.text: Limited exceptions to rule excluding new evidence on judicial review exist but do not apply here
propositions.quote: Although there are certain limited exceptions to the general rule, I am not persuaded that they apply in this matter (see Assn of Universities and Colleges of Canada v Canadian Copyright Licensing Agency, 2012 FCA 22 at paras 19-20).

propositions.text: June 19, 2015 letter is not admissible evidence on judicial review
propositions.quote: Accordingly the June 19, 2015 letter is not admissible.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant's June 19, 2015 letter offering permanent job was not before Officer; new evidence generally inadmissible on judicial review; letter excluded.

propositions.text: Decision-maker presumed to have considered all evidence before him or her
propositions.quote: a decision-maker is presumed to have considered all of the evidence before him or her (Kotanyan v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 507 at para 24).

propositions.text: Officer noted in GCMS Notes that Applicant had valid LMIA with Horizon
propositions.quote: the Officer does note in the GCMS Notes that the Applicant had a valid LMIA with Horizon.

propositions.text: LMIA approval letter was not an offer of employment
propositions.quote: the LMIA approval letter was not an offer of employment.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer presumed to consider all evidence; Officer noted valid LMIA; LMIA letter not an offer of employment.

propositions.text: No merit to Applicant's claim that no legislative basis requires offer of employment
propositions.quote: I do not accept the assertion that there is no legislative basis upon which an offer of employment is required to satisfy the requirements of the IRP Regulations.

propositions.text: Officer relied on s 82 IRP Regulations and s 11.2 IRPA in refusing application, not just policy
propositions.quote: The Officer expressly relied on s 82 of the IRP Regulations and s 11.2 of the IRPA in refusing the application and did not - as asserted by the Applicant - rely only on policy.

propositions.text: s 82 IRP Regulations requires employer to offer arranged employment defined as continuous full-time work for at least one year after visa issuance
propositions.quote: s 82 of the IRP Regulations requires that an employer has offered arranged employment to the applicant, which is defined as an offer of employment “for continuous full-time work in Canada having a duration of at least one year after the date on which a permanent resident visa is issued”.

propositions.text: Officer reasonably required letter of offer to be provided to satisfy arranged employment requirement
propositions.quote: it was reasonable for the Officer to require a letter of offer be provided.

propositions.text: No undue reliance on non-binding policy; refusal under s 11.2 IRPA arose from IRP Regulations requirements
propositions.quote: There was no undue reliance on any non-binding policy considerations, as the Officer’s refusal under s 11.2 arose directly from the requirements of the IRP Regulations.

paragraphs.summary: Court rejects Applicant's claim; Officer relied on s 82 IRP and s 11.2 IRPA; letter of offer reasonably required; no undue reliance on policy.

propositions.text: Applicants must submit documents as requested in checklist; failure may justify denial of permanent residency
propositions.quote: this Court has previously accepted that an applicant is required to submit the documents requested under a document checklist in the form described, and the failure to do so may result in an application for permanent residency being reasonably denied

propositions.text: LMIA letter, checklist, and online instructions informed Applicant of required document to prove arranged employment under s 82
propositions.quote: the LMIA approval letter, document checklist, and online instructions all informed the Applicant of the type of document that was required in order to satisfy the Officer that he had an arranged offer of employment under s 82.

propositions.text: LMIA post-dating invitation is irrelevant; letter required to confirm qualifying offer and validate program requirements
propositions.quote: The fact that the LMIA post-dated the invitation is not relevant. As stated in the online instructions, the purpose of requiring the submission of an offer of employment, in the form described, as a part of the application for permanent residence was to confirm the Applicant’s qualifying offer of arranged employment and to validate that the Applicant met the program requirements.

propositions.text: Officer found Applicant lacked qualifications on basis he was ranked and invitation issued; permanent residence denied under s 11.2 IRPA
propositions.quote: Because the letter containing the relevant information was not provided, the Officer found that the Applicant did not have the qualifications on the basis upon which he was ranked (and qualifying points awarded) and the invitation was issued. Accordingly, pursuant to s 11.2 of the IRPA, permanent residence was denied.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes checklist and instructions required letter proving arranged employment; LMIA date irrelevant; Officer denied residence under s 11.2 IRPA.

propositions.text: Officer could request qualifying offer of employment; duty of fairness did not compel such request
propositions.quote: it was open to the Officer to have requested that the Applicant provide an offer of employment that met the necessary criteria for the reasons set out above, as the duty of procedural fairness owed in the circumstances did not compel the Officer to do so.

propositions.text: Given documents provided, Officer reasonably found no qualifying job offer; decision within acceptable range
propositions.quote: Given the documentation that the Applicant did provide, it was not unreasonable for the Officer to find that this was not sufficient to demonstrate that the Applicant had a qualifying job offer, which determination falls within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes which are defensible in respect of the facts and law.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer could request offer but fairness did not require it; Officer reasonably found no qualifying job offer.

propositions.text: Applicant submits four questions for certification about revoking 600 points and fairness of officer's actions
propositions.quote: The Applicant has submitted the following questions for certification: A. Can an immigration officer revoke 600 points...

paragraphs.summary: Applicant submits four certification questions about revoking points and procedural fairness.

propositions.text: Test for certifying question requires dispositive effect and broad significance beyond immediate parties
propositions.quote: The test for certifying a question is that it “must (i) be dispositive of the appeal and (ii) transcend the interests of the immediate parties to the litigation, as well as contemplate issues of broad significance or general importance” (see Zhang v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FCA 168 at para 9 (“Zhang”)).

propositions.text: Question must have been raised and dealt with by Federal Court judge to be certified
propositions.quote: The question must also have been raised and dealt with by the Federal Court judge (Zhang at para 9).

paragraphs.summary: Court states certification test requires dispositive effect, broad significance, and prior judicial consideration.

propositions.text: None of Applicant's proposed questions meet certification test; not dispositive or broadly significant
propositions.quote: none of the proposed questions meet the test for certification as set out in Zhang. No issues of broad significance or general importance are engaged, nor do the issues proposed by the Applicant transcend the interests of the immediate parties. Moreover, given my findings above, they are not dispositive.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds none of Applicant's questions meet certification test; not dispositive or broadly significant.
